This was the first thriller I have read in quite some time, and for that reason I was a little unsure if it would be for me or not. With that said, I got through the whole book in the course of the day and so I definitely felt compelled to find out what really happened, and I did enjoy the way the author led us on a merry chase before fully revealing things!This is the story of a drowning pool where many women over the years have killed themselves or been killed for being witches. The pool is an area that seems to draw lonely souls and forlorn, troubled people. It's history is so bleak that Nel can't leave the area alone and it becomes an obsession for her to find out the truth behind the lies that surround it. When Nel is found dead floating down the river from the drowning pool the whole of the town is shaken. Not only is it shocking that Nel is dead, it's not been long since a young girl called Katie was also drowned in the pool, and both are at first assumed to be suicides. We follow the police and surrounding family and friends who are left behind to cope with the loss and unanswered questions, and who try to untangle the web of lies...What I really liked about this book was the way that water and the sensual, dark and tricky nature of such an elemental force was a constant theme. The book title is incredibly apt, and the story doesn't shy away from metaphor and meaning, which I actually enjoyed a lot.The young daughter of Nel who is left behind, and her aunt (Nel's estranged sister), were probably the 'main' two, but honestly this book is told from a variety of viewpoints and that added a lot of depth to the mystery. I don't think any of the stories felt uninteresting to me, and I was constantly questioning and second-guessing characters... With that said, I do think that some of the moments in the book felt a little too contrived and predictable, and I didn't feel totally shocked by the revelations at the end becuase many of them I had already worked out.I do feel like this book reads quite like a river flowing. It's twisty and turn-y and filled with misdirection. There's obstacles and there are moments where the current kept me reading and reading, but there are also shallows and moments of calm, and I felt like some of these easier moments let the story down a bit. Overall I am very glad I read the book and I did enjoy the experience of reading a thriller for the first time in a long while. As far as thrillers go I'm not sure how it compares to the others that are out there, but as an exciting read you can get through in a day I do think it's worth trying out. 3*s from me :)

Ooh, a new psychological thriller! I'm gonna buy a ticket for that ride!This book has all the elements of a modern whodunit: a missing woman, adultery, an unreliable narrator and unlikable characters. There is also a train, which is a nice homage to Agatha Christie and Alfred Hitchcock.First, we meet Rachel. The poor woman has a drinking problem, her husband had an affair and left her, and then she lost her job. Rachel is The Girl on the Train — after being fired, she still commutes into London every day, just to wander around and fill the empty hours. At one point, she tells a therapist:"I don't remember things. I black out and I can't remember where I've been or what I've done. Sometimes I wonder if I've done or said terrible things, and I can't remember. And if someone tells me something I've done, it doesn't even feel like me. It doesn't feel like it was me who was doing that thing. And it's so hard to feel responsible for something you don't remember. So I never feel bad enough. I feel bad, but the thing that I've done — it's removed from me. It's like it doesn't belong to me."Rachel is intrigued by a beautiful couple whose home she can see at a stopping point along the route. Every morning, she likes watching the pretty woman on the terrace, and she fantasizes about the happy, romantic life she and her husband must have. The life Rachel no longer has.Then we meet Megan, the pretty woman Rachel likes to daydream about. We quickly learn that Megan's life isn't as perfect as it looks from the outside. (Which reminded me of that saying that you never really know what someone's marriage is like.) Megan is a bit desperate and is looking for a purpose.The story moves along briskly and alternates chapters between the women. Rachel soon finds herself caught in a mystery, but she can't remember what happened because she had been heavily drinking at the time. This book has been getting a lot of hype, some of it justified. The writing is tight, and Paula Hawkins seems to be the new it author, the one who wrote "this year's Gone Girl." (How many more years are we going to hear that phrase? There should be a moratorium.) I did enjoy this thriller, and I gobbled up the last half of the book in one sitting. However, the story did not make any lasting impressions on me. It's a fun ride, but one I'll likely forget as soon as I step off the car.I will say this: the book has a much more satisfying ending than Gone Girl.Favorite Quotes"I am not the girl I used to be. I am no longer desirable, I'm off-putting in some way. It's not just that I've put on weight, or that my face is puffy from the drinking and lack of sleep; it's as if people can see the damage written all over me, can see it in my face, the way I hold myself, the way I move." "I have lost control over everything, even the places in my head." "But I have to do something... All those plans I had — photography courses and cookery classes — when it comes down to it, they feel a bit pointless, as if I'm playing at real life instead of actually living it. I need to find something that I must do, something undeniable. I can't do this, I can't just be a wife. I don't understand how anyone does it — there is literally nothing to do but wait. Wait for a man to come home and love you. Either that or look around for something to distract you."

This book should really be required reading. It sheds light and adds substance to a well-known event of WWII - the atomic bombing of Hiroshima (and Nagasaki). Whether or whether not it was ethically okay to have bombed the cities is debatable, but this book serves to chronicle what enduring the bombing was like through devastating eye-witness accounts. The bombings, despite the fact they occurred seventy years sgo, are becoming increasingly important in a world that concerns itself with the constant development of nuclear weapons. Therefore, this book is important too, perhaps moreso than at its publication date. Yes, it is history, and the past is the past, but as history if such events are not learned, they will be repeated. And, trust me, from what happened in this book, it would be a tragedy.

This is a phenomenal memoir by Trevor Noah. I never wanted the book to end. It had me hanging on every word. I hope Noah does a follow-up that talks about how he ended up on The Daily Show.The book chronicles Noah's often difficult childhood in South Africa. It's both shocking and entertaining. And it was an inspirational look into how one can choose to operate in an oppressive state police and a cultural structure that seeks to suppress freedom and individuality.  “But the highest rung of what’s possible is far beyond the world you can see. My mother showed me what was possible. The thing that always amazed me about her life was that no one showed her. No one chose her. She did it on her own. She found her way through sheer force of will.”  I love how the hero in this book was Trevor’s mom. She is a badass woman and the fact that this book turned into a love letter to his mom was poignant .Highly recommended. Even if you’re not a biographical or non-fiction reader, give this a go. I think you’ll find yourself unable to look away.

Well. That wasn't as good as the first book.Let's start with lack of action; this is sometimes forgivable but seriously, 90% of the book is meetings: conspiracy meetings, counter-conspiracy meetings, meetings about meetings. It's like a Conspiracy Theory Story with very little payoff in terms of action.At best, it feels like an in-between of the first book and what I expect the third book to be. The writing and story has matured since Dune; we'll see how it goes beyond.Honestly though once again the women fall flat. I mean, Chani's nearly the same as in Dune and I know very little about her, her motivations and desires. Hell I still don't know what she looks like, other than "elvin faced" (thankfully he didn't use that term in this book). Alia's probably the best developed female character and she's hard to comprehend.And Paul. I'm bitterly confused, and perhaps I lost the message of the book, it seems just beyond my reach (and that's not an intentional meta-reference). But he at once detests the empire he was unwittingly unleashed across the universe and at the same time viciously protects his line of power. Perhaps from the vacuum that would replace it?Again, it just feels like ends are left for the next book in the series. So all in all, a reasonably readable book, just too long and inert to stand on its own.

Phew! This book is riveting and so very raw. For those who read The Escape Room last year by the same author, expect something very different with this read. This isn't a pulse pounding, fast paced thriller. This is a very heavy and character driven novel touching on the important topic of rape culture.I'm not a podcast person but this book definitely makes me curious to possibly trying one. I enjoyed the podcast transcripts throughout this read (ok, so if podcasts were written, I'd probably read them but still not listen? Haha - it's so hard to say). I also enjoyed the dual timeline and different POVs. We certainly get an in depth look at rape culture and how different (but also the same) it is throughout the years. It was certainly infuriating to get through some of the moments in these pages.“To tell you the truth, I don't get how we can almost unanimously agree that murder is wrong, yet when it comes to rape some people still see shades of gray.”Goldin is clearly a very talented author. I love that the two books I've read so far from her are so very different. I'll certainly be getting The Girl in Kellers Way and keeping an eye out for her next read. I think she handled a very sensitive topic with respect and gave voice to her characters.
